title: This is how I kill cognitive debt, is this how the pros do it?
author: pennystudio
selftext:
[Architectural Diagram](https://preview.redd.it/vqg8b23zeq0h1.png?width=1887&format=png&auto=webp&s=0c9215a513bebb46fbca203208e7b267a76c001e)

I'm vibe coding this game with claude code, the game grew more and more complicated. Despite numerous prompt and invariants I put into the various architectural document and .md files, the code still smells of duplication, parallel path, just doesn't feel clean. 

As a stroke of genius, I thought, what if I ask claude to build me a visualization of the architecture of the game, starting from the game engine, and follow each data path, call sites to its end point? The result is remarkable, I think. 

The diagram is human readable, I can click any block, and it will highlight its connections. Underneath the diagram is json, so it's machine readable, so claude agent could read this and "understand" the architecture instead of reading various documents and code base. 

The moment it's built, it immediately paid dividends. I asked the agent to look at the diagram and spot any architectural gap, they found a few. So I ask the agent to modify the architecteral graph first before changing code. And as I review it, I also spotted a few more architectural gap that we could unify and simplify. For example, I saw a local server and a remote server implementation, that smells like duplication for me. So I ask the agent to build the game with remote PVP first, and fit the offline game in to the mold of the remove server. You paid a small price (miliseconds) of offline performance, but for a turn base game, it's negligible. Then I also spotted the duplication of remote and local client. Same story there. 

At the end, we simplify and unify the architectural a lot. And as a bonus, any future feature add would drive through the architecture graph first, review it, then implement. 

What do you think? Is this how the pros do it? Should I have started with this from the beginning?

comments.author: Hjalm
comments.body: Looks cool! How long did it take to spin this feature up? And any future plans to iterate on this?

replies.author: pennystudio
replies.body: The first version literally just takes minutes for Claude to spin up after I give the intent in the prompt. And immediately I spotted something in the architecture that needs fixing. This is many iterations later with some UI polishes, such as allowing me to drag and reposition the boxes while the connections stay and highlighted. So it's about 1-2 days when it get to this point. So in that time, it's all about doing structural architectural changes with some UI polish for the graph when needed. The cost of building this with AI is really negligible.

comments.author: MythologIQ-Labs
comments.body:
Honestly, this is a really solid instinct.

Maybe the “pro” version has a fancier name, like C4 diagrams, dependency graphs, architecture decision records, or whatever other terminology we invented so engineering could continue pretending diagrams are a separate civilization. But the core idea is right: make the system visible before you keep changing it.

Especially with AI-assisted game dev, I think this matters even more. The model can happily add a new path, duplicate a pattern, or solve the local problem without understanding that it just made the overall architecture worse. A visual graph gives both you and the agent a shared map.

The part I like most is that you’re making the graph part of the workflow instead of just documentation after the fact. “Update/review the architecture first, then change the code” is the important bit. That turns it from a pretty diagram into a guardrail.

For a game, I’d probably want the graph to show a few layers separately:

Game loop / engine flow  
State management  
Networking path  
Save/load path  
UI/input flow  
AI/NPC behavior  
Asset/content pipeline

Because otherwise the graph can become its own little spaghetti monster, just with boxes and lines instead of files.

I don’t think you necessarily needed to start with this on day one. Early prototypes are messy by nature. But once the project starts accumulating systems, this kind of map becomes incredibly useful. The trick is keeping it alive and forcing future features to pass through it before the agent starts spraying code everywhere.

So yes, I think you’re onto something. The real win is not the diagram itself. It’s making architecture review part of the development loop.
